title: 2  The International Monetary System
text:
2.2 Two centuries in one picture





Exhibit 2.1 Two centuries of the international monetary system. Regime boundaries are conventional dates; transitions took years.




Bimetallism and the British exception. The U.S. Coinage Act of 1792 defined the dollar in both gold and silver. Britain drifted onto gold instead, and resumed paying gold for its notes in 1821 after the Napoleonic Wars.
The classical gold standard, 1870s–1914. Once Germany switched to gold after 1871 and the United States resumed convertibility in 1879, the major currencies were fixed to each other through gold: one pound bought $4.8665. Capital moved freely, and London sat at the centre.
Interwar disorder. Gold was suspended in 1914. Britain returned in 1925 at the prewar parity, which overvalued the pound, and was forced off again in 1931. The United States devalued to $35 an ounce in 1934, and the decade dissolved into devaluations and controls.
Bretton Woods, 1944–1973. Currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35. Capital controls made the pegs workable. As dollars piled up abroad, the gold promise became impossible to keep; on 15 August 1971 Nixon closed the gold window, and by 1973 the major currencies floated.
The floating-dollar era. Today the major currencies float, many others still peg, twenty-one European countries share the euro, and the dollar still makes up 57.1 percent of the world’s identified foreign-exchange reserves.

3.1 Why this chapter matters
A currency crisis is what happens when markets stop believing a government’s exchange-rate promise. Reserves drain, interest rates spike, and the peg breaks — usually suddenly, after months in which officials insisted it would hold. A common working definition, from Frankel and Rose (1996), is a depreciation of at least 25 percent in a year that is also at least 10 percentage points faster than the year before.

text:
4.1 Why this chapter matters
Political risk is the chance that a government — the host country’s or your own — or a political event changes what a cross-border investment is worth. Exchange-rate risk can be hedged in a market. Most political risk cannot, which is why firms manage it through structure, contracts and insurance rather than derivatives.

4.3 Measuring it
Two research indexes turn newspaper coverage into a monthly number. The geopolitical risk index of Caldara and Iacoviello counts articles about wars, threats and terrorism, back to 1900.





Exhibit 4.2 Geopolitical risk since 1900. The labels mark the peak month within each episode; compare the two world wars with 2001, 2003 and 2022.




The economic policy uncertainty index of Baker, Bloom and Davis measures something different: uncertainty about what governments will do to taxes, trade, regulation and money.

title: 4  Political Risk in International Finance
text:
4.4 Managing it
Firms have four tools: structure (local partners, local borrowing, staged investment), contracts (bilateral investment treaties and international arbitration), insurance (the World Bank’s MIGA, the U.S. Development Finance Corporation and private insurers) and price (a higher hurdle rate or explicit scenario cash flows).
Running case. Chattanooga Precision Components’ Mexican warehouse faces little expropriation risk. Its bigger exposure is home-government risk: a change in U.S.–Mexico trade terms, such as one arising from the USMCA’s scheduled 2026 joint review, would change the subsidiary’s value without Mexico doing anything at all.






NoteThe Ascent of Money · Niall Ferguson (book, 2008; PBS series)



Watch or read: Chapter 6, “From Empire to Chimerica”, describes how the first age of globalization ended with the outbreak of war in 1914. Ferguson has also published research on the subject: his 2006 Economic History Review article, “Political risk and the international bond market between the 1848 revolution and the outbreak of the First World War”, asks whether bond investors saw the war coming.
What it gets wrong: the book treats 1914 as a single shock. Exhibits 4.2 and 4.3 suggest the modern pattern is different — a rising floor of policy uncertainty rather than one great break.
